talks.title: Joe Gray - NetflOSINT: taking an often-overlooked data source and operationalizing it
talks.teaser: Outlines joe Gray - NetflOSINT: taking an often-overlooked data source and operationalizing it and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: Joe Gray presents at BSides Knoxville on NetflOSINT, operationalizing network flow data as an overlooked but valuable intelligence source for threat hunting.

Key Topics: NetFlow for east-west lateral movement and north-south external communication analysis; limitations of logs as universal truth; NetFlow's resilience against tampering; and practical operationalization approaches.

Technical Details: Gray explains how NetFlow captures communication patterns between hosts that logs may miss or that attackers can alter. He positions flow data as complementary to traditional log analysis for threat hunting.

Takeaways: Network flow data provides tamper-resistant visibility that logs alone cannot guarantee. Threat hunters should incorporate NetFlow analysis into standard investigation workflows.

talks.title: Angie Shue - Defense in Depth for Email Security
talks.teaser: Discusses angie Shue - Defense in Depth for Email Security and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Angie Shue, a cybersecurity engineer at TeamHealth, presents a defense-in-depth architecture for enterprise email security in healthcare, where protected health information (PHI) is heavily targeted. Shue explains the technical integration between cloud email security gateways and on-premises Microsoft Exchange across administrative and clinician domains. She details the coordination of Cisco Secure Email Cloud Gateway (CES) and Armorblox to mitigate advanced phishing, executive impersonation, and internal account compromise.

Key Topics:
- Healthcare-targeted email threats: PHI value, executive impersonation, and recipient-tailored phishing
- Cisco Secure Email Cloud Gateway (CES) multi-stage filtering and Cisco Talos threat intelligence
- Administrative filtering: CLI-based regex message filters, GUI content filters, and outbreak quarantines
- API-driven post-delivery remediation and internal mail inspection using Armorblox via Exchange Web Services (EWS)

Technical Details:
Healthcare organizations face relentless social engineering, from fake delivery notices and voicemail alerts to executive impersonation soliciting wire transfers or gift cards. Because TeamHealth operates an on-premises Microsoft Exchange environment split into an administrative domain and a high-mailbox, low-volume clinician domain, cloud-native security requires hybrid integration. To secure perimeter traffic, TeamHealth deploys Cisco Secure Email Cloud Gateway (CES, formerly IronPort/ESA) across two cloud data centers housing six virtual ESAs and a central Security Management Appliance (SMA), communicating over B2B IPsec VPNs for syslog and LDAP recipient validation (RAD).

Inbound mail traverses sequential inspection stages in CES. Cisco Talos sender reputation scores mail server IPs from -10 to +10; connections scoring below -5 are dropped, scores between -2 and -5 are rate-limited, and scores above +5 pass with standard throughput. CES then validates SPF, DKIM, and DMARC DNS records and applies geolocation filters that drop unauthorized regions (such as Russian mail servers) by default. Next, CLI-configured regex message filters inspect all headers. Cisco's anti-spam engine scores messages from 1 to 100, dropping emails rated 65+ and routing scores 35–65 to junk folders. Attachments are scrutinized by Sophos antivirus and Cisco Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) sandboxing, while outbreak filters temporarily hold suspicious messages until Talos issues updated signatures. If AMP detects a malicious file post-delivery, it leverages EWS APIs through an AWS WAF to execute automated mailbox remediation.

To monitor internal-only traffic and address perimeter bypasses, TeamHealth integrates Armorblox as a secondary layer. Armorblox interfaces directly with on-premises Exchange via EWS APIs. Operating post-delivery, it inspects messages within seconds, executing automated remediation before users open malicious emails. Armorblox also ingests reports from the employee abuse mailbox (reportphishing@teamhealth.com). When analysts confirm a malicious report, Armorblox executes automated bulk deletion across all matching emails organization-wide and maps whether victims forwarded the phishing email internally.

Key Takeaways:
Enterprise email defense requires combining pre-delivery gateway filtering with post-delivery API analysis. Gateways like Cisco CES must enforce strict Sender Reputation thresholds, comprehensive SPF/DKIM/DMARC validation, and attachment sandboxing. Secondary API solutions like Armorblox are essential to inspect internal email for compromised accounts, provide sub-second remediation via EWS, and automate fleet-wide removal of user-reported phishing campaigns.

talks.title: Ross Flynn - Say Hi to the New Guy: How Diverse Backgrounds Can Mature Your Security Program
talks.teaser: Outlines ross Flynn - Say Hi to the New Guy: How Diverse Backgrounds Can Mature Your Security Program and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Ross Flynn, an information security professional with a background in crisis counseling, logistics, and transportation, delivers a presentation at BSides exploring how non-traditional career paths strengthen organizational cybersecurity programs. Flynn addresses the acute talent shortage and industry burnout within security teams, arguing that rigid hiring filters centered exclusively on computer science degrees or standard IT helpdesk progression limit problem-solving capacity. He details the specific operational, cultural, and interpersonal advantages that candidates from diverse career backgrounds contribute to enterprise security operations.

Key Topics:
- Cybersecurity talent acquisition challenges and hiring gatekeeping
- Unique operational perspectives of non-traditional candidates
- Cultural impact, self-directed learning, and remote team dynamics
- Transferable skills: crisis communication, conflict de-escalation, and empathy

Technical Details:
Flynn begins by examining the hiring landscape in cybersecurity, noting that organizations face expanding threat domains—such as those categorized in Henry Zhang’s cybersecurity domain map—yet continue to impose narrow qualifications on entry-level applicants. Standard job descriptions routinely demand five or more years of experience and advanced technical certifications for junior roles, creating unnecessary gatekeeping and reinforcing cognitive homogeneity. Drawing from his personal career transition from commercial truck driving, residential youth management, and logistics coordination into incident response and compliance, Flynn analyzes how non-standard experiences directly address key security challenges.

The presentation details three core areas where non-traditional hires deliver measurable value: perspective, culture, and transferable problem-solving capabilities. From a perspective standpoint, individuals who previously worked in business operations or administrative roles possess intuitive empathy for end users. They understand why employees circumvent cumbersome security controls or fall victim to phishing simulations, allowing security teams to craft realistic training and bridge the persistent cultural divide between IT security and business units. Furthermore, Flynn highlights how crisis counseling methodologies provide vital skills in de-escalating conflicts during audit findings, negotiating risk remediation with recalcitrant stakeholders, and establishing trust during high-stress disaster recovery planning.

Culturally, Flynn argues that hiring managers should prioritize "cultural contribution" over passive "cultural fit." Career changers frequently demonstrate immense personal drive, investing their own time and financial resources into self-directed study, home labs, and foundational training. Introducing this continuous learning mindset helps counter team complacency and cynicism often observed in traditional IT pipelines. He warns against the cognitive trap of the "law of the instrument" (treating every problem like a nail when the only tool is a hammer), demonstrating that non-technical backgrounds foster multi-disciplinary, lateral thinking essential for handling modern, unpredictable incident scenarios.

Key Takeaways:
Security leadership should reform recruiting pipelines by removing arbitrary credential barriers and evaluating candidates on problem-solving aptitude, critical thinking, and communication skills. Incorporating professionals from non-traditional disciplines enhances security culture, reduces adversarial friction between security teams and business units, and improves end-user security awareness programs. Organizations must establish structured onboarding and mentorship programs to rapidly bridge technical domain gaps for high-aptitude career transitioners.

talks.title: Ben Sadeghipour - Would I even be here if it wasn't for the Internet?
talks.teaser: Explores ben Sadeghipour - Would practitioners even be here if it wasnt for the Internet and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## A Personal Keynote

Ben Sadeghipour (better known in bug bounty circles) delivers BSides Knoxville's keynote tracing how the internet shaped his security career. The talk is part autobiography, part encouragement for self-taught hackers navigating an industry that still prizes formal credentials.

## Learning Outside the Classroom

Ben describes struggling with traditional university coursework—failing classes while skipping lectures to learn hacking in the library and on YouTube. Calculus became passable only after finding online tutorials that matched how he actually learns.

## Bug Bounties as a Path In

Platforms like HackerOne offered paid, autonomous practice: no boss, real targets, and money for valid findings. He notes how Yahoo's early $20 gift-card payouts drew community backlash before the program matured into serious rewards.

## Degrees Still Matter

Despite internet-driven success, Ben acknowledges many employers still require CS degrees or extensive experience. His degree ultimately helped open doors, but the internet—and community resources—were what made him a practitioner in the first place.
